startup.name: Scope AR
startup.one_liner: User guided augmented reality tools that give industrial workers the knowledge they need at the point of work.
startup.description: Scope AR sells a licensed product to industrial and field service customers, letting an expert author AR instructions and remote guidance that a worker sees on a tablet or phone while doing repair, assembly or inspection. Customers (equipment makers, utilities, manufacturers) pay a software license. Supporting facts as of Summer 2015: San Francisco team, early pilots, enterprise focus rather than consumer.

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting rate about 1.5 percent for 2015 (Fortune Aug 2015: about 7,000 applicants for about 106 spots; Winter 2015 quoted near 2 percent), inside the repo prior band of 0.6 to 2 percent. Adjustments: enterprise AR with a paid license model and a clear painful workflow is a plus (x1.3), a technical team in a hot 2015 category (Vuforia bought by PTC, Metaio bought by Apple, Meta in YC 2013) is a plus (x1.2), but one thin AR precedent in the YC data and no stated revenue keep it from going higher. Net about 2 percent.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because enterprise AR in mid 2015 depends on headsets and tablets that are not ready, so the pitch looks like a technology demo in search of a buyer. Without paying customers or a founder with deep industrial service experience, the interview reads as an early market bet, and the one earlier YC AR company (Meta) was a hardware story that needed far more capital.

bands.rationale: Small seed or angel round only, the thin band for a company that gets modest pilots.
Typical 2013 to 2017 YC seed, median about 2.4M in the cohort.
Upside band if a marquee industrial customer lands, in a hot 2015 AR climate.

ladder.why_it_fails: Seed fails if pilots do not turn into paid licenses before the YC bump fades. Investors in 2015 saw enterprise AR as early, with Vuforia and Metaio as platform risks. Analogs Meta and VizeraLabs raised seed but struggled afterwards, and Zigfu, a layer on Kinect, found no durable buyer, so a team without a named paying customer gets passed.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Below the anchor because enterprise AR needs a repeatable sales motion that few 2015 companies could show by month 27, and because AR hardware (HoloLens, tablets) was not yet mass market.

bands.rationale: Thin A, small by cohort standards where the median 2013 to 2017 A is about 7.5M.
Standard A for a software license business with several paying accounts.
Upside if AR hardware matures and a strategic investor joins.

ladder.why_it_fails: The Series A is missed if revenue stays at pilot size and each customer needs custom content work. Investors then see a services business, not software. Avametric reached an exit but not a big round, and VizeraLabs, a projector AR company, never moved past seed. Platform shifts by PTC or Apple could also turn the product into a feature.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Below the anchor since the survivor base in the cohort skews to software winners, and an enterprise AR vendor needs expensive field sales and integration work to scale.

bands.rationale: Small B, the thin band if growth is slow.
Typical B, median about 19.5M in the cohort, with higher figures for hot sectors.
Upside if the company is the category leader for industrial AR.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B fails if growth is linear and customer concentration stays high. Industrial buyers move slowly, so annual recurring revenue may not reach the level needed. Meta raised a B in 2016 on hardware hype and later collapsed, which shows that a round alone does not mean a durable business. Larger players with bundled AR would compete on price.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Below the anchor since few enterprise AR companies exist at that scale in 2015 and the cohort has n=12 only, so the rate is an anecdote.

bands.rationale: Modest Series C or growth round for a company with steady but not explosive industrial AR revenue.
Typical Series C, since the 2013 to 2017 cohort median C is about 80M dollars (n=2, an anecdote).
Upside if AR becomes a standard industrial tool.

ladder.why_it_fails: Reaching a Series C needs a clear leadership position in a market that was barely formed in 2015. Large industrial software vendors can bundle AR with their own platforms and have the customer relationships. If AR adoption moves slower than hoped, growth investors pass and the company seeks a sale instead, as many YC companies in the cohort did.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely the company does not reach a large exit because enterprise AR in 2015 is early, device-dependent and crowded by platform owners such as PTC with Vuforia and Apple with Metaio. In the 2005 to 2014 YC cohort 46 percent shut down and only a few reached over 1B. A mid size sale to an industrial software vendor is the likelier good outcome, with a shutdown the single biggest branch.

analogs.outcome_summary: Raised a 23M Series A and 50M Series B, then collapsed in 2018 after a lead investor withdrew.

Summer 2011 layer above Kinect, a developer tool on a hardware platform.
analogs.outcome_summary: Shut down, depended on a single device platform.

analogs.relevance: Winter 2014 body simulation using 3D, a software license style business.

killers.risk: Platform owners absorb enterprise AR (PTC Vuforia, Apple Metaio, Microsoft HoloLens)
killers.evidence: PTC bought the Vuforia platform in 2015 for about 65 million dollars and incumbents have the customer lists.
killers.mitigation: Be device agnostic and own the authoring and workflow data.

killers.risk: Pilots do not become paid licenses; sales cycles are long
killers.evidence: Industrial buyers run pilots for many months, and a services heavy deal looks like consulting to investors.
killers.mitigation: Sell a narrow repair workflow with a measured saving and charge from day one.

killers.risk: Devices and tracking are not ready, so the experience disappoints
killers.evidence: Tablet based AR in 2015 has weak tracking, and head mounted devices are not yet sold at scale.
killers.mitigation: Ship on phones and tablets today and avoid dependence on headsets.

killers.risk: Market too small or too early to support venture scale
killers.evidence: Analyst interest in enterprise AR is rising but spend is small in 2015.
killers.mitigation: Expand from guided repair to training and quality inspection.

competition_now.name: PTC Vuforia
competition_now.what: AR platform acquired by PTC in 2015, tied to its IoT and PLM products.
competition_now.traction: Developer base of large size and large industrial customers at PTC.

competition_now.name: Metaio
competition_now.what: German AR software company with a development toolkit for enterprise and marketing.
competition_now.traction: Established vendor with industrial customers in Europe before Apple bought it in 2015.

competition_now.name: Status quo: paper manuals, phone calls to experts, and videos
competition_now.what: How most field workers get help in 2015.

technical_complexity.rationale: Robust marker free tracking, content authoring tools and cloud management are hard, and a small team can build a narrow guided repair app in three months but not a full platform. Dependence on tablet cameras and later headsets adds hardware risk.

takeover_risk.rationale: Platform companies and PLM vendors have the distribution and incentive and can add AR guidance within 12 to 24 months. Zigfu and Meta show platform and hardware dependency has hurt past YC AR companies.

evidence.claim: PTC bought the Vuforia AR platform in 2015, signalling large industrial vendors see demand for AR in service.
Industry consortia such as AREA formed to push enterprise AR adoption, showing interest but early spend.

actions: Close one paid pilot with a named equipment maker.
Record the measured time saved per repair.
roadmap.proof: One signed paid pilot with a measured saving.

actions: Package a narrow repair workflow as a fixed price license.
Run on tablets and phones with no new hardware.
roadmap.proof: Three paying accounts and 100K dollars of recurring revenue.

actions: Hire an industrial sales lead and a solutions engineer.
Reduce custom content work with authoring tools.
roadmap.proof: Annual recurring revenue near 1M dollars with gross margin above 70 percent.

pros.point: Clear paid use case in industrial service
pros.evidence: Customers already pay for training and field support, and large vendors such as PTC are moving into AR.

pros.point: Enterprise license model avoids consumer retention risk
pros.evidence: B2B cohort in 2005 to 2014 reached seed at 95 percent and series A at 70 percent conditionally, above the broad cohort.

brand.rationale: The name is short and descriptive and the name cohort rates sit near the average, so it is neutral. A descriptor name limits pivots, as with other YC compound names, and it will not drive growth.

narrative.headline: A plausible but long shot enterprise AR company: about 2 percent to get into YC and roughly 3 percent to reach Series C.
narrative.general_summary: Scope AR is a 2015 enterprise augmented reality product for guiding workers through repair and assembly. The need is real, since field service is costly and large vendors such as PTC are buying AR capability, but the market is early, devices are immature and platform owners can copy the idea. The YC cohort from 2005 to 2014 shows that about 46 percent of companies shut down and 29 percent reach Series B, with B2B doing better than consumer. We give the company a base rate position with a small discount for the early market and takeover risk.

assumptions: Described only from the YC directory one-liner, description and 2015 web context; no traction figures were available so none are assumed.
Base rate cohort is 2005 to 2014 (n=79, calibration only); the narrow Consumer cohort had 23 companies, so B2B (n=41) was used instead and its small size is noted.
Knowledge coverage: researched companies are about 10 percent of the directory; funding is incomplete so lower, known and upper ranges apply.
Hindsight leak: running yc_overlap.py printed this company's directory outcome line; the estimates were set from base rates and kept unchanged by it.
Comps.py returned mostly post 2015 companies; only analogs founded before 2015 were used.
